extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors, applicants, and patent practitioners involved in §101 analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the two-part Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility analysis (including Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B) focusing on improvements, particular machines/transformations, and conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification shows improvement to technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art; a conclusory, bare assertion of an improvement without necessary detail is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indication that the claimed invention provides an improvement can include a discussion in the specification that identifies a technical problem and explains the details of an unconventional technical solution expressed in the claim, or identifies technical improvements realized by the claim over the prior art. Examples: McRO (specification explained how rules automated animation tasks); contrast Affinity Labs (failure to provide details was dispositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim reflects the disclosed improvement (claim-as-a-whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding the specification discloses an improvement, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement in technology; the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim itself does not need to explicitly recite the improvement (e.g., 'thereby increasing the bandwidth of the channel'), but the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) should be considered. Evaluate the claim 'as a whole,' i.e., 'as an ordered combination, without the requirements of individual steps.' Be careful to avoid oversimplifying claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for specific claim requirements (citing Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec and McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of claimed solution vs claiming an idea/outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve an outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or the outcome itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with 'particular machine' and 'mere instructions to apply an exception' analyses; evaluation of those considerations may assist in determining whether a claim satisfies the improvement consideration (citing McRO and DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and admissible evidence for showing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners generally are not expected to make qualitative judgments on the merits of an asserted improvement; if the examiner concludes the disclosed invention does not improve technology, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive arguments supported by necessary evidence under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 must establish what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill in the art and cannot be used to supplement the specification (see MPEP § 716.09 for § 1.132 practice). Example: applicants may submit declarations explaining how one skilled in the art would understand the disclosed improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functionality (vs computer as tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (an improvement to computer functionality) or merely invokes a computer as a tool to perform an existing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: Enfish (improved way computer stores/retrieves data demonstrated eligibility) contrasted with cases where a computer was merely added post-hoc. The claim should show a specific implementation of a solution to a software problem rather than a generic addition of a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may show improvement in computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-identified illustrative examples of improvements that may demonstrate improved computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes (i) modification of hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages (DDR Holdings), (ii) inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter Internet content (BASCOM), (iii) method of rendering halftone digital image (Research Corp.), (iv) unconventional distributed network architecture to reduce congestion (Amdocs), (v) memory system configurable by processor type (Visual Memory), (vi) technical details for transmitting images or appending classification info (TLI Communications — note this case found insufficiency), (vii) particular server structure storing organized digital images (TLI Communications — use of generic server insufficient), (viii) particular programming/design for software menus (Apple v. Ameranth), (ix) method generating security profile improving virus protection (Finjan), (x) improved user interface showing selectable summary (Core Wireless), (xi) specific interface and implementation for 3D spreadsheets (Data Engine), (xii) specific method of restricting software operation within a license (Ancora).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope must be limited to computer implementation to show computer improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A method claim's broadest reasonable interpretation must be limited to computer implementation to be considered an improvement to computer technology; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Synopsys (method could be performed mentally — ineligible), RecogniCorp (process practicable verbally/telephone — ineligible). If a claimed process covers both computer and non-computer embodiments, it may fail to improve computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative examples: insufficient to show computer-functionality improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative examples where courts found claimed subject matter did not amount to an improvement in computer functionality or technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth), (ii) speeding up analysis solely by virtue of general-purpose computer (FairWarning), (iii) mere automation of manual processes on generic computers (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving images using conventional tech without technical details (TLI Communications), (v) affixing barcode without technical limitations (Secured Mail Solutions), (vi) instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve it (Interval Licensing), (vii) improving information stored by a database is not necessarily improving database functionality (BSG Tech), (viii) arranging GUI info to assist traders (Trading Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in non-computer technologies also count
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of improvements applies regardless of the technology; improvements in life sciences or other technical fields may demonstrate eligibility so long as they improve technology rather than merely an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rapid Litigation Management (preserving hepatocytes was an improvement). However, an improvement in an abstract idea (e.g., a better economic concept) is not an improvement in technology (Trading Technologies). McRO (animation rules improved animation technology) is cited as non-computer-specific precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may show improvement in other technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-identified illustrative examples where improvements outside core computer-functionality demonstrated eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes (i) computerized modification of rubber-molding press using thermocouple (Diehr), (ii) new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), (iii) advance in downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs), (iv) particular digital data compression methods (DDR Holdings; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec), (v) incorporating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec), (vi) measurement devices/techniques generating new data (Electric Power Group), (vii) configuration/methods using inertial sensors (Thales Visionix), (viii) structured GUI improving trader accuracy (Trading Techs. Int’l v. CQG), (ix) improved hepatocyte preservation (CellzDirect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require details how computer aids method; mere generic computer additions insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that computer involvement assists in improving technology, claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which it aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method; merely adding generic computer components is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on generic components or machinery. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for 'mere instructions to apply an exception' guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation is a useful clue but not a standalone test
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful and important clue and investigative tool when determining patent eligibility, but it is not a stand-alone test and does not supersede the Alice/Mayo framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims must be evaluated under the two-part Alice/Mayo test: if a claim passes Alice/Mayo it is eligible even if it 'fails' the M-or-T test; if a claim fails Alice/Mayo it is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test (citing Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine/apparatus elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether a recited machine provides 'significantly more,' consider how specifically the machine or its elements are identified in the claim (not 'any and all machines').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mackay Radio (claim recited particular antenna shape/angles) and Eibel Process (particular Fourdrinier machine structure). A general-purpose computer performing conventional functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial; TLI Communications; Eon v. AT&T). If applicant adds generic computer elements and asserts 'programmed' or 'particular machine,' examiner should determine whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the machine is integral to achieving performance of the claimed method (plays a significant part) versus being merely an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of a machine may integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more; mere use of the Internet or a machine as a data source/object often will not (CyberSource). Versata explains that for a machine to add significantly more, it must 'play a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed, rather than function solely as an obvious mechanism for permitting a solution to be achieved more quickly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine involvement as extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the recited machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim (i.e., whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution (e.g., only a data gathering step or field-of-use limitation) will not integrate the judicial exception or provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (transformation of a particular article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a clue that the claim may integrate an exception into a practical application or be 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of an article (physical object/substance) to a different state or thing is relevant, but the M-or-T test is not standalone. Courts cite Gottschalk v. Benson and Gottschalk/Corning examples. Purely mental processes and mere manipulation of abstract data are not eligible transformations (CyberSource; Warmerdam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation must be of a particular article; not mental/data-only
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance; transformations of purely mental processes or mere manipulation of mathematical/data constructs are not considered eligible transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing location alone is usually insufficient; evidence that the transformed article has a new/different function or use supports that a true transformation occurred. Examples: Tilghman v. Proctor (fat/water heated to produce fat acids/glycerine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors relevant to transformation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate these specific factors when a transformation is recited: (1) particularity/generality of the transformation, (2) degree to which the recited article is particular, (3) nature/extent of change in state or thing, (4) nature of the article transformed (physical v. intangible), (5) whether transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More particular transformations and transformations of particular physical articles that result in different function/use are more likely to provide significantly more. Transformations that are generic, apply to any article, or only change location are less likely. See discussion and Mayo example where administering a drug was considered only a field-of-use and insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry; such elements do not add 'significantly more' to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is evaluated only in Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis. If additional elements are merely routine or conventional, they will generally not transform an otherwise ineligible claim into eligible subject matter.
